title: Who Is This? The Christ, the Cross, and the Road to Jerusalem
summary: Jesus sends out the Twelve, Herod wonders who he is, and Jesus feeds five thousand people from five loaves and two fish. Peter confesses him as the Christ of God, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer and that followers must take up their cross daily. On a mountain he is transfigured before three disciples; afterward he heals a boy, rebukes the disciples' ambitions, and sets his face toward Jerusalem, warning would-be followers of the cost.
story: This chapter is the hinge of Luke's Gospel. The question that has been building since chapter 5 (“Who is this?”) is asked by Herod, answered by Peter, and confirmed by the Father's voice on the mountain. Once Jesus' identity is confessed, he reveals his destiny: rejection, death, and resurrection. Then, at verse 51, Luke begins a long section (running to about 19:27) in which Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, where that destiny waits. Much of Jesus' most famous teaching in Luke, including the Good Samaritan and the lost son, is set along this road. The Galilean ministry closes; the road to the cross opens.
historical:
Herod the tetrarch is Antipas, who had John beheaded; Mark 6:14-29 tells that story at length, while Luke mentions it only in passing. Antipas's anxious curiosity pays off later, when he finally meets Jesus at his trial (23:8-12). Bethsaida lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee on the northeast, in the territory of Herod Philip, who raised it to the status of a city and renamed it Julias in honor of the emperor's family.

Between the feeding (Mark 6:30-44) and Peter's confession (Mark 8:27-30), Mark includes a long stretch of material that Luke leaves out entirely, and scholars sometimes call this Luke's great omission. The effect is to bring the feeding and the confession close together. The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Galilee and Judea. They traced their descent to the old northern tribes of Israel, accepted only the five books of Moses, and worshiped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem; the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple there in the late second century BC. Hostility between the two peoples was deep, and Josephus records later clashes when Galileans passed through Samaria on the way to festivals in Jerusalem.
cultural:
The Twelve were to travel light and depend on the hospitality of those who welcomed them, a common expectation for wandering teachers. Shaking dust from the feet was a public sign of breaking off responsibility. When crucifixion was the Roman punishment for rebels and slaves, and condemned men carried their crossbeams to the place of execution, Jesus' call to take up a cross would have sounded shocking, not religious. Luke's word daily turns it into the shape of a whole life.

Peter's offer to build three shelters recalls the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in temporary shelters to remember the wilderness years and looked forward to God's future. Burying a father was among the most sacred duties of a son in Jewish life, taking precedence over many other commandments. Some suggest the man meant he would follow after his father's eventual death, or after the year-long wait before the bones were gathered into a bone box (ossuary), a practice of the period; either way, Jesus' reply claims a priority higher than the strongest family duty. The plow saying recalls Elisha, who asked to say goodbye to his parents before following Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21).
literary: Herod's question in verse 9 (“who is this man I hear such things about?”) and the list of popular opinions in verses 7-8 and 19 frame Peter's confession. The chapter then turns on the passion predictions in verses 22 and 44. The transfiguration echoes Moses on Sinai: a mountain, a changed face, a cloud, a voice, and a command to listen, which recalls Moses' promise of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15). Only Luke tells us that Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' departure, using the Greek word exodos. The final section begins with a solemn phrase (literally, he set his face to go to Jerusalem) that recalls the resolve of the Servant in Isaiah 50:7. Parallels are found in Mark 6, 8, and 9 and Matthew 14, 16, 17, and 8:19-22.

outline.t: Peter's confession and the first passion prediction
A boy healed and a second passion prediction
Setting out for Jerusalem; a Samaritan village refuses

doctrines.note: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ of God, and Jesus immediately defines what that means: a Messiah who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and be raised. The title is true, but the popular expectation of it must be remade by the cross.
The Son of Man must suffer. The word must signals divine necessity: Jesus' death is not an accident of politics but the accomplishment of God's plan, the departure he will fulfill at Jerusalem.

Discipleship is defined here: self-denial, a daily cross, welcoming the least, refusing rivalry and revenge, and putting Jesus above every other claim. The community that follows him is shaped by his road.

words.note: Exodos, departure or exit, sometimes used for death. Luke's choice is deliberate: it is the title given in the Greek Old Testament to the book of Exodus. Jesus' death, resurrection, and ascension at Jerusalem will be a new exodus, God's great act of rescue for his people.

Stauros, cross, the upright stake and crossbeam used by Rome for executions meant to shame. To take up a cross meant to walk toward one's own death. Jesus uses it of discipleship before he carries his own.

Arneomai, to deny or disown. To deny oneself is to refuse the self's claim to be master. The same verb describes Peter's later denial of Jesus (22:57): a disciple either says no to the self or, under pressure, says no to Jesus.

Analepsis, a taking up. It points to Jesus' ascension, which Luke narrates at the end of the Gospel and the start of Acts, and it sums up the whole movement of death, resurrection, and exaltation that begins with the turn toward Jerusalem.

christ: Here Jesus is identified by the church's first confession (the Christ of God) and by the Father's own words (“This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!”). The transfiguration gives the three disciples a glimpse of the glory that belongs to him, and Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, talk with him about his death. The feeding of the five thousand shows him as the one who provides for God's people in the wilderness as God gave manna, and his taking, blessing, breaking, and giving anticipate the Last Supper (22:19). Yet this glorious Son sets his face toward Jerusalem to be delivered into human hands. Luke's picture holds glory and suffering together: the way to the glory the disciples glimpsed runs through the cross.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not die before they saw the kingdom of God (verse 27)?
hard.a: If the saying refers to the final coming of the kingdom at the end of history, it seems not to have happened in the disciples' lifetime. Interpreters have offered several readings. Many from the early church onward connect it with the transfiguration, which Luke places immediately after it: some of the disciples (Peter, James, and John) saw the kingdom's glory within days. Others point to the resurrection, ascension, and outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, when the kingdom came in power, as Luke describes in Acts. Others link it to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 as a visible act of judgment. Luke's wording, see the kingdom of God, is simpler than Mark's (the kingdom come with power), which fits the reading that the disciples would witness the kingdom's arrival in Jesus' own ministry and victory. Most readers see these as overlapping rather than competing answers.

questions: Jesus asks his disciples, “Who do you say I am?” How would you answer in your own words, and how has your answer changed over time?
Luke adds the word daily to Jesus' call to take up the cross. What would a daily cross look like in an ordinary week of your life?
James and John wanted to call down fire on a village that rejected Jesus. How do followers of Jesus today respond when people reject him, and how does his rebuke apply?
